newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Historic chemical weapons ban set to go into force.
newsitem.headline: Historic chemical weapons ban set to go into force.

text.p: A landmark convention banning the development, production, stockpiling and use of chemical weapons will enter into force on April 29, 1997 after Hungary became the 65th country to ratify the accord, a U.N. spokesman said on Thursday.

The Chemical Weapons Convention, which also calls for the destruction of chemical weapons and their production facilities, has been signed by 160 countries. It enters into force 180 days after receipt by the United Nations of the 65th ratification.

The convention, which is of unlimited duration, has so far been signed by 160 countries including all five permanent members of the Security Council -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France. But among them only Britain and France have so far ratified the accord.
It was opened for signature in Paris by Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali in January 1993.

In a statement after receiving Hungary's ratification, the U.N. chief said: "The world has taken a significant step toward the complete eradication of chemical weapons. The United Nations welcomes the efforts of member states to outlaw the barbaric and indiscriminate horror of chemical warfare."
Boutros-Ghali hailed October 31 as "a special day for the United Nations in our continuing efforts to further the cause of global disarmament."

He urged all states that had not yet ratified the accord, "and particularly those with significant chemical weapons stockpiles, to join those that have already done so, and to give full meaning to this historic agreement."
The convention is the first disarmament agreement negotiated in a multilateral framework that provides for the elimination of an entire category of weapons of mass destruction.
It was the result of a decade of negotiations in the Conference on Disarmament, the international community's main disarmament negotiating body.

A similar convention prohibiting the development, production and stockpiling of bacteriological weapons entered into force in 1975 and was regarded as a possible first step towards a comprehensive chemical weapons ban.
Although a 1925 agreement called the Geneva Protocol prohibits the use in war of asphyxiating, poisonous or other gases, it did not forbid their development, production, stockpiling or deployment.
Gas was first used on a large scale as a weapon during World War One and more, recently, it was used during the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war.

A U.N. special commission set up after the 1991 Gulf War is still checking that Iraq's stocks of chemical weapons have all been destroyed, as well as its nuclear, biological and ballistic missile potential.
Thousands of U.S. and other allied troops suffered ill-effects known as "Gulf War syndrome" when Iraqi chemical weapons stocks were destroyed at the end of the Gulf War.
An organisation headquartered at The Hague, assisted by a technical secretariat, will be responsible for verifying the provisions of the Chemical Weapons Convention are carried out.

Each state party undertakes never to develop, produce, otherwise acquire, stockpile or retain chemical weapons, or transfer them to anyone. They promise never to use chemical weapons and never to engage in any military preparations to use them.
Each party also undertakes to destroy chemical weapons and production facilities. Destruction must be completed no later than 10 years after the convention's entry into force.
